statements.statement: If \(K\) is a compact subset of a Euclidean space, the hyperspace \(\mathcal H(K)\) of its closed subsets, with the empty set isolated and the Hausdorff metric on nonempty members, is compact.  The extended diameter is continuous on \(\mathcal H(K)\).
statements.proof_tex:
Consider any sequence \((C_j)\) in \(\mathcal H(K)\).  If infinitely many terms are empty, that subsequence converges to the isolated empty set.  Otherwise discard finitely many terms and assume all \(C_j\) are nonempty.  Let \((x_r)_{r\ge1}\) be a countable dense subset of \(K\).  The numbers \(d(x_r,C_j)\) lie in the compact interval \([0,\operatorname{diam}(K)]\).  Successive subsequence extraction and a diagonal argument give a subsequence along which they converge for every \(r\).  Since every function \(x\mapsto d(x,C_j)\) is one-Lipschitz, a finite-net argument upgrades convergence on the dense set to uniform convergence on \(K\); call the limit \(f\).

Choose \(z_j\in C_j\).  Compactness gives a further subsequence with \(z_j\to z\in K\), and uniform convergence implies \(f(z)=0\).  Thus \(C=\{x\in K:f(x)=0\}\) is nonempty and closed.  The one-Lipschitz property gives \(f(x)\le d(x,C)\).  Conversely, choose \(z_j(x)\in C_j\) with \(\|x-z_j(x)\|=d(x,C_j)\), pass to a convergent subsequence, and use uniform convergence to see that its limit lies in \(C\); hence \(d(x,C)\le f(x)\).  Therefore \(f=d(\,cdot\,,C)\).  Uniform convergence of distance functions for nonempty compact sets is equivalent to Hausdorff convergence, since
\[
 d_H(C_j,C)=\sup_{x\in K}|d(x,C_j)-d(x,C)|.
\]
Every sequence thus has a convergent subsequence, and the metrizable hyperspace is compact.  Finally, for nonempty \(C,D\),
\[
 |\operatorname{diam}(C)-\operatorname{diam}(D)|\le2d_H(C,D).
\]
Continuity at the isolated empty set is automatic under the convention \(\operatorname{diam}(\varnothing)=0\).  This proves both assertions.

statements.statement:
Fix \(s_0\) with \(\Gamma(s_0)=\{\tau_0\}\) and \(R\in(0,\infty)\).  Put \(K_R=\bigcup_{(b,h)\in\Lambda_R}\{\eta_b(h)\}\) and let \(\mathcal H_R\) be the compact hyperspace of closed subsets of \(K_R\), including the empty set.  If \(\varphi_h\) is the \(\mathcal N(h,V_0)\) density, then \(v_R<\infty\), the infimum defining \(v_R\) is attained, and it has the explicit semi-infinite linear-program characterization
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_R=\min_{t,Q}\quad &t\\
\text{subject to}\quad
&Q(\,\cdot\mid y)\in\mathcal P(\mathcal H_R)\text{ measurably in }y,\\
&\int_{\mathbb R^d}\!\int_{\mathcal H_R}
  {\bf1}\{\eta_b(h)\in C\}\,Q(dC\mid y)\varphi_h(y)\,dy
  \ge1-\gamma,\quad (b,h)\in\Lambda_R,\\
&\int_{\mathbb R^d}\!\int_{\mathcal H_R}
  \operatorname{diam}(C)\,Q(dC\mid y)\varphi_h(y)\,dy
  \le t,\quad (b,h)\in\Lambda_R.
\end{aligned}
\]
After the coverage-preserving and diameter-nonincreasing truncation \(C\mapsto C\cap K_R\), the attaining \(\mathcal H_R\)-valued randomized confidence rules are exactly the measurable uniform-randomizer realizations of the minimizing kernels \(Q\), up to null sets.  In particular, every unrestricted attaining rule has an \(\mathcal H_R\)-valued truncation represented by a minimizing kernel, although the unrestricted rule itself need not be supported on \(\mathcal H_R\).  This local characterization does not by itself settle finite-sample dominance: changing any proposed pullback at one fixed sample size leaves all its local asymptotic limits unchanged while it can destroy coverage or diameter dominance at that sample size.
statements.proof_tex:
Because \(\Gamma(s_0)=\{\tau_0\}\), the accessible branch set \(\mathbb B(s_0)\) is nonempty; it is finite because \(\mathbb B_p\) is finite.  For \(b\in\mathbb B(s_0)\), define
\[
 L_{b,R}=T_b(s_0)\cap\{h\in\mathbb R^d:\|h\|_2\le R\}.
\]
Because \(b\in\mathbb B(s_0)\), the point \(s_0\) belongs to \(\overline{\mathcal S_b}\); hence the zero direction belongs to \(T_b(s_0)\), so \(L_{b,R}\) is nonempty.  The tangent cone \(T_b(s_0)\) is closed by definition, and the closed radius-\(R\) Euclidean ball is compact because \(R<\infty\).  Hence \(L_{b,R}\) is compact.  The map \(\eta_b(h)=D\theta_b(s_0)h\) is linear and therefore continuous.  By the definition of \(\Lambda_R\),
\[
 K_R=\bigcup_{b\in\mathbb B(s_0)}\eta_b(L_{b,R}).
\]
This is a finite union of compact subsets of \(\mathbb R^3\), and thus is compact.  In particular,
\[
 D_R:=\operatorname{diam}(K_R)<\infty.
\tag{1}
\]

We first justify the reduction to the compact action space \(\mathcal H_R\).  For a closed set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^3\), put
\[
 T(C)=C\cap K_R.
\tag{2}
\]
The map \(T\) is measurable from the Effros sigma-field on closed subsets of \(\mathbb R^3\) to the Borel sigma-field of \(\mathcal H_R\).  Indeed, let \(O=K_R\cap G\), where \(G\subseteq\mathbb R^3\) is open, and define
\[
 A_m=\{x\in K_R:\operatorname{dist}(x,G^c)\ge m^{-1}\},\qquad m\ge1.
\]
With \(A_1=K_R\) when \(G^c=\varnothing\), the sets \(A_m\) are compact and \(O=\bigcup_{m\ge1}A_m\).  For every compact \(A\subseteq\mathbb R^3\), closedness of \(C\) and compactness of \(A\) imply
\[
 \{C:C\cap A\ne\varnothing\}
 =\bigcap_{\ell\ge1}\{C:C\cap A^{1/\ell}\ne\varnothing\},
\tag{3}
\]
where \(A^{1/\ell}\) is the open \(1/\ell\)-neighborhood of \(A\).  Thus compact-hit events are Effros measurable.  Consequently
\[
 \{C:T(C)\cap O\ne\varnothing\}
 =\bigcup_{m\ge1}\{C:C\cap A_m\ne\varnothing\}
\tag{4}
\]
is measurable, and, for open \(O\subseteq K_R\),
\[
 \{C:T(C)\subseteq O\}
 =\{C:C\cap(K_R\setminus O)=\varnothing\}
\tag{5}
\]
is measurable because \(K_R\setminus O\) is compact.  We now verify directly that these events suffice for the Hausdorff Borel sigma-field.  Fix a nonempty \(A\in\mathcal H_R\), \(r>0\), and a countable dense sequence \((a_i)_{i\ge1}\) in \(A\).  For every nonempty closed \(D\subseteq K_R\),
\[
 d_H(D,A)<r
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 D\subseteq A^r
 \ \text{and}\ 
 \sup_{i\ge1}\operatorname{dist}(a_i,D)<r,
\tag{5a}
\]
because distance to a nonempty closed set is continuous and the supremum over compact \(A\) equals the supremum over its dense sequence.  Moreover,
\[
 \left\{C:\sup_{i\ge1}\operatorname{dist}(a_i,T(C))<r\right\}
 =\bigcup_{\substack{q\in\mathbb Q\\0<q<r}}
   \bigcap_{i\ge1}
   \left\{C:C\cap K_R\cap\overline B(a_i,q)\ne\varnothing\right\}.
\tag{5b}
\]
Every hit set on the right of (5b) is measurable by (3), while the containment condition in (5a) is measurable by (5).  Thus the preimage under \(T\) of every nonempty Hausdorff open ball is measurable.  The preimage of the isolated empty member of \(\mathcal H_R\) is \(\{C:C\cap K_R=\varnothing\}\), which is measurable by (3).  Hausdorff open balls and that isolated singleton generate the Borel sigma-field of \(\mathcal H_R\), proving measurability of \(T\).

For every \((b,h)\in\Lambda_R\), the target \(\eta_b(h)\) belongs to \(K_R\).  Therefore, pointwise in every closed \(C\),
\[
 {\bf1}\{\eta_b(h)\in T(C)\}={\bf1}\{\eta_b(h)\in C\},
 \qquad
 \operatorname{diam}(T(C))\le\operatorname{diam}(C).
\tag{6}
\]
Thus truncation preserves every coverage probability and cannot increase any expected-diameter risk.  The unrestricted infimum \(v_R\) therefore equals the infimum over \(\mathcal H_R\)-valued rules: one inequality follows because those rules are a subclass, and the reverse inequality follows by applying \(T\) to every unrestricted rule.  By \(\text{lem:hyperspace-compactness}\), \(\mathcal H_R\) is compact and \(C\mapsto\operatorname{diam}(C)\) is continuous on it.

We next obtain a common dominating law.  The matrix \(V_0\) is positive definite.  To verify this from its displayed covariance formula, let \(c\ne0\) be a vector in half-vector coordinates and let \(A_c\ne0\) be the corresponding symmetric coefficient matrix, with its off-diagonal entries normalized so that contraction with a symmetric matrix agrees with contraction by \(c\).  Expanding
\[
 V(\Sigma)_{AB,CD}=\Sigma_{AC}\Sigma_{BD}+\Sigma_{AD}\Sigma_{BC}
\]
gives
\[
 c^{\mathsf T}V(\Sigma)c
 =2\operatorname{tr}\!\left\{(\Sigma^{1/2}A_c\Sigma^{1/2})^2\right\}>0
\tag{7}
\]
for every positive-definite \(\Sigma\): the symmetric matrix \(\Sigma^{1/2}A_c\Sigma^{1/2}\) is nonzero, so the trace of its square is strictly positive.  The two covariance matrices encoded by \(s_0\in\Omega_p\) are positive definite, and \(\lambda\in(0,1)\).  Hence the block-diagonal definition of \(V_0\), together with (7), proves \(V_0\succ0\).

Let \(\varphi_0\) be the \(\mathcal N(0,V_0)\) density and put \(\mu_0=\mathcal N(0,V_0)\).  For every \(h\in\mathbb R^d\), completing the square in the two nonsingular Gaussian densities gives the continuous, strictly positive Radon--Nikodym derivative
\[
 w_h(y):=\frac{\varphi_h(y)}{\varphi_0(y)}
 =\exp\!\left\{h^{\mathsf T}V_0^{-1}y
 -\frac12h^{\mathsf T}V_0^{-1}h\right\},
 \qquad
 \int w_h\,d\mu_0=1.
\tag{8}
\]

Let \(\delta\) be an \(\mathcal H_R\)-valued randomized rule.  Its joint measurability and the independence and uniformity of \(U\) induce the probability kernel
\[
 Q(A\mid y)=\int_0^1{\bf1}\{\delta(y,u)\in A\}\,du,
 \qquad A\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H_R).
\tag{9}
\]
Conversely, \(\text{lem:kernel-uniform-randomization}\) realizes every probability kernel from \(\mathbb R^d\) to the standard Borel space \(\mathcal H_R\) as a jointly measurable function of \((y,U)\).  Since \(w_h\varphi_0=\varphi_h\), change of measure shows that, for each \(k=(b,h)\in\Lambda_R\), the coverage and risk of \(Q\) are
\[
 G_k(Q)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\!\int_{\mathcal H_R}
 {\bf1}\{\eta_b(h)\in C\}\,Q(dC\mid y)\varphi_h(y)\,dy
\tag{10}
\]
and
\[
 L_k(Q)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\!\int_{\mathcal H_R}
 \operatorname{diam}(C)\,Q(dC\mid y)\varphi_h(y)\,dy.
\tag{11}
\]
It follows from (9)--(11) that the feasible kernels are exactly those satisfying \(G_k(Q)\ge1-\gamma\) for every \(k\in\Lambda_R\), and the least feasible epigraph coordinate for a fixed kernel is \(\sup_{k\in\Lambda_R}L_k(Q)\).  This proves equality between the decision problem and the displayed semi-infinite linear program, apart from attainment.  The constant rule \(C=K_R\) has coverage one and, by (1), risk \(D_R\).  Therefore
\[
 0\le v_R\le D_R<\infty.
\tag{12}
\]

It remains to prove attainment.  For every integer \(j\ge1\), the definition of the infimum and (12) permit a feasible kernel \(Q_j\) such that
\[
 \sup_{k\in\Lambda_R}L_k(Q_j)\le v_R+j^{-1}.
\tag{13}
\]
Define a probability measure on \(\mathbb R^d\times\mathcal H_R\) by
\[
 \zeta_j(dy,dC)=\mu_0(dy)Q_j(dC\mid y).
\tag{14}
\]
Every \(\zeta_j\) has first marginal \(\mu_0\), and its second coordinate belongs to compact \(\mathcal H_R\).  Given \(\epsilon>0\), choose a compact Euclidean ball \(L_\epsilon\) with \(\mu_0(L_\epsilon)>1-\epsilon\).  Then
\[
 \zeta_j(L_\epsilon\times\mathcal H_R)>1-\epsilon
\tag{15}
\]
for every \(j\), so \((\zeta_j)_{j\ge1}\) is tight.  The product \(\mathbb R^d\times\mathcal H_R\) is a separable complete metric space.  By \(\text{lem:prokhorov-tightness}\), a subsequence, not relabeled, converges weakly to a probability measure \(\zeta\).

For every bounded continuous \(g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\), weak convergence and the common first marginal give
\[
 \int g(y)\,\zeta(dy,dC)
 =\lim_{j\to\infty}\int g(y)\,\zeta_j(dy,dC)
 =\int g(y)\,\mu_0(dy).
\tag{16}
\]
Thus the first marginal of \(\zeta\) is \(\mu_0\).  Both factors are standard Borel spaces, so \(\text{lem:standard-borel-disintegration}\) supplies a probability kernel \(Q\) satisfying
\[
 \zeta(dy,dC)=\mu_0(dy)Q(dC\mid y).
\tag{17}
\]

Fix \(k=(b,h)\in\Lambda_R\) and define
\[
 F_k=\{(y,C)\in\mathbb R^d\times\mathcal H_R:\eta_b(h)\in C\}.
\tag{18}
\]
The set \(F_k\) is closed because membership of a fixed point is preserved under Hausdorff convergence and the empty member is isolated.  For \(L>0\), let \(w_h^L=w_h\wedge L\).  Since \(w_h^L\) is nonnegative and continuous and \({\bf1}_{F_k}\) is upper semicontinuous, \(w_h^L{\bf1}_{F_k}\) is bounded and upper semicontinuous.  Feasibility of \(Q_j\), (8), (10), and the common first marginal in (14) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \int w_h^L{\bf1}_{F_k}\,d\zeta_j
 &=\int w_h{\bf1}_{F_k}\,d\zeta_j
   -\int(w_h-w_h^L){\bf1}_{F_k}\,d\zeta_j\\
 &\ge1-\gamma-\int(w_h-w_h^L)\,d\mu_0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{19}
\]
The upper-semicontinuous Portmanteau inequality \(\text{lem:portmanteau-usc}\) therefore yields
\[
 \int w_h^L{\bf1}_{F_k}\,d\zeta
 \ge\limsup_{j\to\infty}\int w_h^L{\bf1}_{F_k}\,d\zeta_j
 \ge1-\gamma-\int(w_h-w_h^L)\,d\mu_0.
\tag{20}
\]
By (8),
\[
 0\le\int(w_h-w_h^L)\,d\mu_0
 \le\int_{\{w_h>L\}}w_h\,d\mu_0\longrightarrow0.
\tag{21}
\]
Monotone convergence as \(L\to\infty\), followed by (17) and (20)--(21), proves
\[
 G_k(Q)=\int w_h{\bf1}_{F_k}\,d\zeta\ge1-\gamma.
\tag{22}
\]
Since \(k\) was arbitrary, \(Q\) satisfies every coverage constraint.

For risk, the function
\[
 (y,C)\longmapsto w_h^L(y)\operatorname{diam}(C)
\]
is bounded and continuous by \(\text{lem:hyperspace-compactness}\).  Weak convergence therefore implies
\[
 \int w_h^L(y)\operatorname{diam}(C)\,d\zeta
 =\lim_{j\to\infty}
 \int w_h^L(y)\operatorname{diam}(C)\,d\zeta_j.
\tag{23}
\]
Because \(\zeta_j\) and \(\zeta\) all have first marginal \(\mu_0\), while \(0\le\operatorname{diam}(C)\le D_R\) on \(\mathcal H_R\), replacing \(w_h^L\) by \(w_h\) in any integral in (23) changes it by at most
\[
 D_R\int(w_h-w_h^L)\,d\mu_0\longrightarrow0,
\tag{24}
\]
uniformly in \(j\).  Equations (13), (23), and (24) consequently imply
\[
 L_k(Q)=\lim_{j\to\infty}L_k(Q_j)\le v_R.
\tag{25}
\]
This holds for every \(k\in\Lambda_R\), so \(\sup_kL_k(Q)\le v_R\).  The kernel \(Q\) is feasible by (22), and \(v_R\) is the infimum over feasible rules.  Therefore
\[
 \sup_{k\in\Lambda_R}L_k(Q)=v_R.
\tag{26}
\]
Equations (10)--(13) and (26) prove attainment and the exact minimum characterization in the displayed semi-infinite linear program.

By \(\text{lem:kernel-uniform-randomization}\), every minimizing kernel has a measurable realization using \(U\), and that realization is an attaining \(\mathcal H_R\)-valued rule.  Conversely, the kernel induced through (9) by any attaining \(\mathcal H_R\)-valued rule satisfies the program constraints and has epigraph value \(v_R\), so it is minimizing.  The likelihood ratios in (8) are everywhere strictly positive and finite.  Hence all Gaussian-shift laws have the same null sets as \(\mu_0\), proving the stated qualification up to null sets.  If an unrestricted rule attains \(v_R\), its measurable truncation \(T\circ\delta\) remains feasible by (6) and has risk at most \(v_R\).  The definition of the infimum forces equality, and the kernel induced by this truncation is therefore minimizing.

Finally, the local characterization cannot by itself imply an all-sample finite-sample comparison.  Let \((\Delta_N)_{N\ge1}\) be any proposed sequence of finite-sample pullbacks and fix one sample size \(N_0\).  Replacing only \(\Delta_{N_0}\) by the constantly empty set leaves \(\Delta_N\) unchanged for every \(N>N_0\), and therefore leaves every local asymptotic limit unchanged, but its coverage at \(N_0\) is zero.  Alternatively, replacing only \(\Delta_{N_0}\) by the constant set \(\mathbb R^3\) again leaves every local asymptotic limit unchanged, while its diameter at \(N_0\) is \(+\infty\).  Thus this local minimax characterization establishes neither finite-sample coverage nor finite-sample diameter dominance for an arbitrary pullback.
statements.justification: Compact hyperspace and kernel arguments establish existence and an exact variational benchmark for randomized closed confidence sets in the discontinuous branch-labelled Gaussian shift experiment.
statements.gap: Geyer1994Constrained treats constrained-estimator cone asymptotics, while Strieder--Drton and Wang--Kolar--Drton treat different structure-uncertainty procedures; none proves this branchwise-coverage kernel semi-infinite-linear-program attainment result.
statements.consumer: The result benchmarks candidate boundary procedures, but provides no explicit minimizing rule, solved value, or finite-sample dominance conclusion.

statements.statement:
The Gaussian boundary class is a subclass of the full Bystrova--Devijver anchor class:
\[
 \mathcal M_p^{\mathrm{df}}\subseteq\mathcal M_p^{\mathrm{BD}}.
\]
In particular, membership in \(\mathcal M_p^{\mathrm{df}}\) entails invariance of the full exogenous distribution, not merely equality of its coordinate variances.
statements.proof_tex:
Take \(M\in\mathcal M_p^{\mathrm{df}}\).  By \(\text{def:boundary-model-class}\), the model satisfies \(\text{ass:linear-structural-equations}\), \(\text{ass:baseline-parent-containment}\), \(\text{ass:modular-interventions}\), and \(\text{ass:diff-faithfulness}\), which are the four shared structural conditions in \(\text{def:bystrova-devijver-anchor-class}\).  It remains to verify causal sufficiency and invariance of the entire exogenous law.

By \(\text{ass:independent-gaussian-innovations}\), for each \(e\in\mathbb E\),
\[
 \varepsilon_e\sim\mathcal N(0,\operatorname{diag}(\omega)).
\]
By \(\text{ass:positive-innovation-variances}\), every \(\omega_v\) is strictly positive, so this law has density
\[
 f_e(x)=\prod_{v\in\mathbb V}
 (2\pi\omega_v)^{-1/2}
 \exp\!\left(-\frac{x_v^2}{2\omega_v}\right).
\]
The displayed product factorization proves that the coordinates of \(\varepsilon_e\) are mutually independent.  Thus the innovations are causally sufficient in the sense required by the anchor class.  By \(\text{ass:invariant-innovation-variances}\), the same vector \(\omega\) occurs in both environments.  The displayed density is therefore identical for \(e=1\) and \(e=2\), proving
\[
 \operatorname{Law}(\varepsilon_1)=\operatorname{Law}(\varepsilon_2).
\]
All defining conditions of \(\mathcal M_p^{\mathrm{BD}}\) now hold, so \(M\in\mathcal M_p^{\mathrm{BD}}\).  Since \(M\) was arbitrary, the asserted inclusion follows.

statements.statement:
For every integer \(p\ge3\) and every \((a,b)\) in the chain--fork parameter space, let \((D_N)\) be a confidence procedure satisfying
\[
 \inf_{M\in\mathcal M_p^{\mathrm{BD}}}
 \Pr_M\{\tau(M)\in D_N\}\ge 1-\gamma
\]
for every \(N\).  Then, under the common sample law of the \(p\)-dimensional chain and fork witnesses in \(\text{def:chain-fork-witness}\),
\[
 \Pr\{\operatorname{diam}(D_N)\ge\sqrt2|a|\}\ge1-2\gamma
\]
for every \(N\).  Thus, in every dimension \(p\ge3\), the same-law noncontraction bound applies to uniform honesty over the full, not necessarily Gaussian, Bystrova--Devijver anchor class.
statements.proof_tex:
Fix an integer \(p\ge3\) and nonzero \(a,b\).  By \(\text{thm:honesty-noncontraction-lower-bound}\), the corrected chain and fork witnesses are members of \(\mathcal M_p^{\mathrm{df}}\), have the same complete sample law, and have target vectors at Euclidean distance \(\sqrt2|a|\).  The inclusion
\[
 \mathcal M_p^{\mathrm{df}}\subseteq\mathcal M_p^{\mathrm{BD}}
\]
from \(\text{lem:gaussian-subclass-of-anchor}\) puts both witnesses in the full anchor class.  The displayed uniform-coverage premise therefore gives coverage at least \(1-\gamma\) at each witness.  Applying the two-model conclusion of \(\text{thm:honesty-noncontraction-lower-bound}\) under their common law gives
\[
 \Pr\!\left\{\operatorname{diam}(D_N)\ge\sqrt2|a|\right\}\ge1-2\gamma
\]
for every admissible \(N\).  Neither the inclusion nor the same-law argument imposes a bound on \(|a|\), and \(p\ge3\) was arbitrary.
statements.justification: Uniform honesty over a class must cover every Gaussian witness in its subclass, so the same-law two-point argument yields the identical finite-sample diameter bound.
statements.gap: The published anchor class has a population discovery theorem but no confidence-set noncontraction converse for an environment-specific direct-effect triple.
statements.consumer: The lower-bound interpretation remains valid even when the intended scientific model class permits non-Gaussian exogenous distributions.

statements.statement:
Fix any integer \(p\ge3\), and let \(\mathcal C\) be either \(\mathcal M_p^{\mathrm{df}}\) or \(\mathcal M_p^{\mathrm{BD}}\).  For every \(N\), every confidence procedure satisfying
\[
 \inf_{M\in\mathcal C}\Pr_M\{\tau(M)\in D_N\}\ge1-\gamma
\]
obeys
\[
 \sup_{M\in\mathcal C}\mathbb E_M\!\left[\operatorname{diam}(D_N)\right]=\infty.
\]
Consequently the infimum of this worst-case expected diameter over all such globally honest procedures is infinite for every \(p\ge3\).  By contrast, for every declared bounded tangent experiment with \(R\in(0,\infty)\), \(\text{thm:local-minimax-attainment-characterization}\) gives \(v_R<\infty\) and attainment.  Thus the theory has a dimension-uniform global-unbounded versus bounded-local elbow.
statements.proof_tex:
Fix an integer \(p\ge3\), an admissible total sample size \(N\), and first take \(\mathcal C=\mathcal M_p^{\mathrm{df}}\).  Set \(b=1\).  For every \(a\neq0\), global honesty supplies the two coverage inequalities required by \(\text{thm:honesty-noncontraction-lower-bound}\).  Under the common sample law \(Q_{N,a}\) of the corresponding \(p\)-dimensional witnesses, that theorem gives
\[
 Q_{N,a}\!\left\{\operatorname{diam}(D_N)\ge\sqrt2|a|\right\}\ge1-2\gamma.
\]
For any nonnegative extended random variable \(T\) and \(t>0\), the pointwise inequality \(T\ge t\mathbf 1\{T\ge t\}\) and monotonicity of integration imply
\[
 \mathbb E[T]\ge t\Pr\{T\ge t\}.
\]
Apply this identity with \(T=\operatorname{diam}(D_N)\) and \(t=\sqrt2|a|\).  Since either witness belongs to \(\mathcal C\) and has sample law \(Q_{N,a}\),
\[
 \sup_{M\in\mathcal C}\mathbb E_M\!\left[\operatorname{diam}(D_N)\right]
 \ge \sqrt2|a|(1-2\gamma).
\]
The assumption \(\gamma\in(0,1/2)\) makes \(1-2\gamma>0\).  The model class places no upper bound on \(|a|\), and the witness remains positive definite for every finite \(a\), so letting \(|a|\to\infty\) proves that the supremum is \(+\infty\).

For \(\mathcal C=\mathcal M_p^{\mathrm{BD}}\), the same argument invokes \(\text{thm:anchor-class-honesty-noncontraction}\), which supplies the identical tail inequality for every \(a\neq0\).  Thus every globally honest procedure has infinite worst-case expected diameter for either class.  The collection over which the infimum is taken is nonempty: the constant closed-set rule \(D_N=\mathbb R^3\) is sample-measurable and has coverage one, although its extended diameter is infinite.  Since every member of this nonempty collection has worst-case expected diameter \(+\infty\), its infimum is \(+\infty\).

Finally, for every declared bounded tangent experiment and every \(R\in(0,\infty)\), \(\text{thm:local-minimax-attainment-characterization}\) proves \(v_R<\infty\) and produces an attaining randomized confidence rule.  Combining that finite attained local value with the global conclusion above proves the asserted elbow for every \(p\ge3\).
statements.justification: This proposition states the final scale comparison required by the rescaled witness: global uniform honesty has infinite minimax expected diameter, whereas each bounded tangent experiment has a finite attained value.
statements.gap: Existing post-selection and structure-union methods do not provide this global-unbounded versus bounded-local characterization for a paired environment-specific direct-effect triple.
statements.consumer: It tells users that no globally narrow honest procedure exists without restricting the model scale, while local bounded-radius optimality remains mathematically meaningful.

statements.statement: Every semialgebraic set admits a finite Whitney stratification by Nash manifolds. For a Nash mapping between Nash manifolds, the set of critical values is semialgebraic and has dimension strictly smaller than the target manifold.

source.locator: Sections 2.8, 9.1, 9.6, and 9.7, dimension, Sard, and Whitney-stratification results
source.verbatim_statement: For a Nash mapping between Nash manifolds, the critical values form a semi-algebraic subset of the target of smaller dimension. Every Nash stratification of a semi-algebraic set has a finer Nash stratification satisfying Whitney conditions a and b.

statements.statement:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be closed and semialgebraic, and let \(E\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be compact, full-dimensional, semialgebraic, and regular closed, meaning \(E=\overline{\operatorname{int}E}\). Outside a semialgebraic Lebesgue-null set of translations \(y\),
\[
 C\cap(y+E)=\overline{C\cap(y+\operatorname{int}E)}.
\]
At every such \(y\), put \(D=y+E\). Let \(C_n\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be closed sets converging locally in the Painleve--Kuratowski topology to \(C\), and let \(D_n=y_n+E_n\subseteq\mathbb R^d\). Assume \(\limsup_nD_n\subseteq D\), every compact \(K\subseteq y+\operatorname{int}E\) is contained in \(D_n\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), and there is a compact \(K_0\) containing \(C_n\cap D_n\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). Then \(\overline{C_n\cap D_n}\to C\cap D\) in the Fell topology, with Hausdorff convergence whenever the limiting intersection is nonempty.
statements.proof_tex:
Put \(D=y+E\).  We first identify the exceptional translations.  By \(\text{lem:semialgebraic-stratification-sard}\), choose finite Whitney stratifications of \(C\) and \(\partial E\) by Nash manifolds, say \((S_j)_j\) and \((R_\ell)_\ell\).  For every pair of strata define the Nash map
\[
 F_{j\ell}:S_j\times R_\ell\longrightarrow\mathbb R^d,
 \qquad F_{j\ell}(c,e)=c-e.
\]
The product is a Nash manifold and the displayed map is the restriction of polynomial subtraction.  Hence \(\text{lem:semialgebraic-stratification-sard}\) says that its critical-value set \(B_{j\ell}\) is semialgebraic and has dimension strictly smaller than \(d\).  It consequently has empty interior and is contained in its boundary, so \(\text{lem:semialgebraic-boundary-null}\) gives Lebesgue measure zero.  Thus
\[
 B:=\bigcup_{j,\ell}B_{j\ell}
 \tag{1}
\]
is a semialgebraic Lebesgue-null set.

Fix \(y\notin B\).  If \(x\in C\cap(y+\partial E)\), choose the unique strata containing \(x\) and \(x-y\).  Since \(y=F_{j\ell}(x,x-y)\) is a regular value, the derivative of subtraction is onto, equivalently
\[
 T_xS_j+T_{x-y}R_\ell=\mathbb R^d.
 \tag{2}
\]
Here is the local consequence of (2) that is needed below.  In Nash charts at \(x\) and \(x-y\), choose a linear complement of \(T_{x-y}R_\ell\) inside the image of \(T_xS_j\).  Solving the corresponding normal-coordinate equations (the derivative in those selected coordinates is invertible by (2)) shows that the normal projection of \(S_j-y\) contains a neighborhood of the normal coordinate of \(R_\ell\).  The Whitney local product structure, together with \(E=\overline{\operatorname{int}E}\), then supplies points
\[
 x_r\in S_j\cap(y+\operatorname{int}E),
 \qquad x_r\longrightarrow x.
 \tag{3}
\]
For completeness, if \(R_\ell\) is zero-dimensional, (2) forces \(T_xS_j=\mathbb R^d\), so \(S_j\) is locally open and (3) follows directly from regular closedness of \(E\).  Points already in \(C\cap(y+\operatorname{int}E)\) need no approximation.  Therefore
\[
 C\cap D=\overline{C\cap\operatorname{int}D}.
 \tag{4}
\]

Now put \(A_n=\overline{C_n\cap D_n}\) and \(A=C\cap D\).  To prove the upper set limit, take any subsequence, still indexed by \(n\), and points \(x_n\in A_n\) with \(x_n\to x\).  Choose \(z_n\in C_n\cap D_n\) with \(\lVert z_n-x_n\rVert\le n^{-1}\).  Local Painlev\'e--Kuratowski upper convergence of \(C_n\), and the assumed inclusion \(\limsup_nD_n\subseteq D\), imply
\[
 x=\lim_nz_n\in C\cap D=A.
 \tag{5}
\]
Thus \(\limsup_nA_n\subseteq A\).

For the lower set limit, fix \(x\in A\).  By (4), choose \(x^{(r)}\in C\cap\operatorname{int}D\) with \(x^{(r)}\to x\).  Choose \(\varepsilon_r>0\) such that
\[
 K_r:=\overline B(x^{(r)},\varepsilon_r)
 \subseteq\operatorname{int}D.
 \tag{6}
\]
Local Painlev\'e--Kuratowski lower convergence gives \(x_n^{(r)}\in C_n\) with \(x_n^{(r)}\to x^{(r)}\).  For each fixed \(r\), eventually \(x_n^{(r)}\in K_r\), while the stated erosion hypothesis applied to the compact set \(K_r\) gives \(K_r\subseteq D_n\) eventually.  Hence \(x_n^{(r)}\in C_n\cap D_n\) eventually.  A diagonal choice, first in \(n\) and then in \(r\), produces points of \(A_n\) converging to \(x\), and therefore
\[
 A\subseteq\liminf_nA_n.
 \tag{7}
\]
Equations (5)--(7) prove Painlev\'e--Kuratowski, hence Fell, convergence \(A_n\to A\).

Finally, the common-compact-bound hypothesis places every sufficiently large \(A_n\) in one compact set.  If \(A=\varnothing\) and infinitely many \(A_n\) were nonempty, compactness would produce a convergent subsequence of selected points, contradicting (5); hence \(A_n=\varnothing\) eventually.  If \(A\ne\varnothing\), upper and lower convergence inside that common compact set are equivalent to Hausdorff convergence.  This proves all assertions.

statements.statement: For every \(b\in\mathbb B_p\), the rational predecessor-regression map \(\theta_b\) on \(\mathcal S_b\) has a \(C^\infty\) extension to all of \(\Omega_p\). More precisely, each environment-specific nonzero direct-effect coordinate is a polynomial divided by a positive-definite principal minor of the corresponding covariance matrix, coordinates fixed to zero extend as zero, and the third coordinate is the difference of the first two. Consequently every \(\theta_b\) is continuously differentiable, with a uniform first-order Taylor expansion on compact local-coordinate sets, at every \(s_0\in\overline{\mathcal S_b}\cap\Omega_p\).
statements.proof_tex:
Fix \(b\in\mathbb B_p\). The finite enumeration in \(\text{thm:finite-branch-representation}\) fixes, in each environment \(e\), a predecessor set \(P_{e,b}\) for \(Y\), the position of \(X\), and whether the \(X\to Y\) coefficient is constrained to be zero. If it is constrained to zero, extend that coordinate by the constant zero function. Otherwise \(X\in P_{e,b}\), and the Cholesky predecessor regression gives
\[
 \alpha_{e,b}(\Sigma_e)
 =e_{X,P_{e,b}}^{\mathsf T}
   \Sigma_{e,P_{e,b}P_{e,b}}^{-1}
   \Sigma_{e,P_{e,b}Y}
 =\frac{q_{e,b}(\Sigma_e)}
        {\det(\Sigma_{e,P_{e,b}P_{e,b}})},
 \tag{1}
\]
where \(e_{X,P_{e,b}}\) is the coordinate vector selecting \(X\) and \(q_{e,b}\) is a polynomial, by the adjugate identity \(A^{-1}=\operatorname{adj}(A)/\det(A)\). For every \(s\in\Omega_p\), the matrix \(\Sigma_e\) is positive definite. Its principal submatrix \(\Sigma_{e,P_{e,b}P_{e,b}}\) is therefore positive definite, and hence
\[
 \det(\Sigma_{e,P_{e,b}P_{e,b}})>0.
 \tag{2}
\]
Thus the right side of (1) is a rational function with nowhere-vanishing denominator on the open set \(\Omega_p\), so it is \(C^\infty\) there. The branch triple is
\[
 \theta_b(s)=
 \bigl(\alpha_{1,b}(\Sigma_1),
       \alpha_{2,b}(\Sigma_2),
       \alpha_{1,b}(\Sigma_1)-\alpha_{2,b}(\Sigma_2)\bigr),
 \tag{3}
\]
and is therefore \(C^\infty\) on \(\Omega_p\).

Now fix \(s_0\in\overline{\mathcal S_b}\cap\Omega_p\) and a compact set \(K\subset\mathbb R^d\). Openness of \(\Omega_p\) implies that \(s_0+t u\in\Omega_p\) for all \(u\in K\) and all sufficiently small \(|t|\). Continuity of the first derivative on a compact neighborhood gives
\[
 \sup_{u\in K}\|\theta_b(s_0+t u)-\theta_b(s_0)\|=O(|t|),
 \tag{4}
\]
and continuity of the derivative, through the integral remainder formula, gives
\[
 \sup_{u\in K}
 \frac{\|\theta_b(s_0+t u)-\theta_b(s_0)
 -tD\theta_b(s_0)u\|}{|t|}=o(1).
 \tag{5}
\]
Equations (4)--(5) are the asserted uniform continuity and first-order Taylor properties. They were derived from positive definiteness and the rational branch representation, not imposed as a separate regularity assumption.
statements.justification: The rational predecessor-regression representation supplies the smoothness needed for both orders of the boundary limit, so it need not be assumed.
statements.gap: This is an internal regularity discharge: positivity of every covariance principal minor turns the branch formulas into globally smooth rational maps on the positive-definite covariance domain.
statements.consumer: The boundary limit theorem and the regular-stratum reduction use the resulting uniform Taylor expansion.

statements.statement:
For every \(B\ge1\), put
\[
K_B=2B^2+4,
\qquad
\kappa_B=K_B^{-2},
\]
and define
\[
\mathcal M_{p,B}^{\mathrm{df}}
=\left\{M\in\mathcal M_p^{\mathrm{df}}:
\max_{e\in\mathbb E}\max_{u,v\in\mathbb V}|B_{e,uv}|\le B,
\quad
\kappa_B I_p\preceq\Sigma_{M,e}\preceq K_BI_p
\ \text{for every }e\in\mathbb E\right\}.
\]
For \(s\in\Omega_p\), let
\[
\Psi_B(s)
=\overline{\{\tau(M'):M'\in\mathfrak F(s)\cap
\mathcal M_{p,B}^{\mathrm{df}}\}},
\]
and project the same paired exact Wishart region through this restricted fiber:
\[
\widehat{\mathcal C}^{B}_{n,\gamma}
=\overline{\bigcup_{s:\operatorname{vech}^{-1}(s)\in
\mathcal R_{n,\gamma}}\Psi_B(s)}.
\]
Then, for every integer \(p\ge3\), every \(n_1,n_2>p\), and every \(0<\gamma<1/2\),
\[
\inf_{M\in\mathcal M_{p,B}^{\mathrm{df}}}
\Pr_M\{\tau(M)\in\widehat{\mathcal C}^{B}_{n,\gamma}\}
\ge1-\gamma.
\]
Moreover, with the infimum below taken over all possibly randomized, \(\mathcal Z_n\)-measurable closed-set-valued rules \(D\) satisfying the displayed uniform coverage constraint, and with the extended-diameter convention \(\operatorname{diam}(\varnothing)=0\),
\[
\sqrt2 B(1-2\gamma)
\le
\inf_{\substack{D:\ 
 \inf_{M\in\mathcal M_{p,B}^{\mathrm{df}}}
 \Pr_M\{\tau(M)\in D\}\ge1-\gamma}}
\sup_{M\in\mathcal M_{p,B}^{\mathrm{df}}}
\mathbb E_M[\operatorname{diam}(D)]
\le
\sup_{M\in\mathcal M_{p,B}^{\mathrm{df}}}
\mathbb E_M[\operatorname{diam}(\widehat{\mathcal C}^{B}_{n,\gamma})]
\le2\sqrt6 B.
\]
Consequently the bounded projected-Wishart union is finite-sample constant-factor minimax for expected diameter, with factor at most \(2\sqrt3/(1-2\gamma)\).  This assertion is neither exact minimax optimality nor attainment of the minimax infimum, and it asserts no rate in the sample sizes.
statements.proof_tex:
Fix \(B\ge1\), \(p\ge3\), \(n_1,n_2>p\), and \(0<\gamma<1/2\), and use the notation introduced in the statement.

First consider coverage.  If \(M\in\mathcal M_{p,B}^{\mathrm{df}}\), then \(M\in\mathcal M_p^{\mathrm{df}}\).  Therefore \(\text{lem:true-completion-retention}\) gives
\[
M\in\mathfrak F(s(M)).
\]
Membership of \(M\) in the bounded class then strengthens this to
\[
M\in\mathfrak F(s(M))\cap\mathcal M_{p,B}^{\mathrm{df}},
\qquad
\tau(M)\in\Psi_B(s(M)).
\]
By \(\text{lem:wishart-pivot}\), the event
\[
E_M=\{\boldsymbol\Sigma_M\in\mathcal R_{n,\gamma}\}
\]
has probability exactly \(1-\gamma\).  On \(E_M\), the definition of \(\widehat{\mathcal C}^{B}_{n,\gamma}\) includes the coordinate \(s(M)\) in its union, and hence
\[
E_M\subseteq
\{\tau(M)\in\widehat{\mathcal C}^{B}_{n,\gamma}\}.
\]
It follows that
\[
\Pr_M\{\tau(M)\in\widehat{\mathcal C}^{B}_{n,\gamma}\}
\ge1-\gamma.
\]
Taking the infimum over \(M\in\mathcal M_{p,B}^{\mathrm{df}}\) proves the finite-sample coverage assertion.  This is the same exact-pivot argument as in \(\text{thm:finite-sample-honesty}\), now with true-completion retention checked in the restricted fiber; it uses no separation or beta-min margin.

We next verify that the same-law witnesses required for the lower bound belong to the bounded class.  Specialize \(\text{def:chain-fork-witness}\) and \(\text{thm:honesty-noncontraction-lower-bound}\) to
\[
a=B,
\qquad
b=1.
\]
These values lie in the chain--fork parameter space because \(B\ge1\).  In the chain model the only nonzero structural coefficients are \(B\) and \(1\).  In the fork model they are \(B/(B^2+1)\) and \(1\).  Since
\[
0<\frac{B}{B^2+1}\le B
\quad\text{and}\quad
1\le B,
\]
every environment coefficient in both models has absolute value at most \(B\).

The common three-dimensional covariance of the witnesses is
\[
\Sigma^{\mathrm{cf}}(B,1)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&B&B\\
B&B^2+1&B^2+1\\
B&B^2+1&B^2+2
\end{pmatrix}
=LL^{\mathsf T},
\qquad
L=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&0&0\\
B&1&0\\
B&1&1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The triangular matrix \(L\) has unit diagonal.  Hence \(\Sigma^{\mathrm{cf}}(B,1)\) is positive definite and
\[
\det\Sigma^{\mathrm{cf}}(B,1)=(\det L)^2=1,
\qquad
\operatorname{tr}\Sigma^{\mathrm{cf}}(B,1)=2B^2+4=K_B.
\]
Let \(0<\lambda_1\le\lambda_2\le\lambda_3\) be its eigenvalues.  Positivity and the trace identity imply \(\lambda_j\le K_B\) for all \(j\).  The determinant identity then gives
\[
\lambda_1=\frac{1}{\lambda_2\lambda_3}
\ge\frac{1}{K_B^2}=\kappa_B.
\]
Thus
\[
\kappa_B I_3\preceq\Sigma^{\mathrm{cf}}(B,1)
\preceq K_B I_3.
\]
For \(p>3\), \(\text{def:chain-fork-witness}\) appends the identity block \(I_{p-3}\).  Since \(K_B\ge6\) and \(0<\kappa_B\le1\), the appended unit eigenvalues also lie in \([\kappa_B,K_B]\); for \(p=3\) the appended block is empty.  Therefore the full covariance in each environment of each witness obeys
\[
\kappa_B I_p\preceq
\Sigma^{\mathrm{cf}}(B,1)\oplus I_{p-3}
\preceq K_B I_p.
\]
The established same-law theorem already proves that both witnesses are in \(\mathcal M_p^{\mathrm{df}}\).  Together with the coefficient and covariance checks above, this proves
\[
M^{\mathrm{ch}},M^{\mathrm{fk}}
\in\mathcal M_{p,B}^{\mathrm{df}}.
\]

Now let \(D\) be any rule in the minimax infimum.  The two witnesses induce the same law pair by \(\text{thm:honesty-noncontraction-lower-bound}\); \(\text{ass:independent-gaussian-sampling}\) therefore makes their complete sample laws identical.  If \(D\) uses an independent auxiliary randomizer, adjoining that same randomizer preserves equality of the two laws.  Denote the resulting common law by \(Q\).  The witness targets are
\[
t_{\mathrm{ch}}=(B,B,0),
\qquad
t_{\mathrm{fk}}=(0,0,0),
\qquad
\|t_{\mathrm{ch}}-t_{\mathrm{fk}}\|_2=\sqrt2 B.
\]
Because both witnesses belong to the bounded class, uniform coverage of \(D\) gives
\[
Q\{t_{\mathrm{ch}}\in D\}\ge1-\gamma,
\qquad
Q\{t_{\mathrm{fk}}\in D\}\ge1-\gamma.
\]
The elementary union bound yields
\[
Q\{t_{\mathrm{ch}},t_{\mathrm{fk}}\in D\}
\ge1-2\gamma.
\]
On this event the definition of diameter gives \(\operatorname{diam}(D)\ge\sqrt2 B\).  Since diameter is nonnegative, including when it takes the value \(+\infty\),
\[
\mathbb E_Q[\operatorname{diam}(D)]
\ge \sqrt2 B\,
Q\{\operatorname{diam}(D)\ge\sqrt2 B\}
\ge\sqrt2 B(1-2\gamma).
\]
Consequently
\[
\sup_{M\in\mathcal M_{p,B}^{\mathrm{df}}}
\mathbb E_M[\operatorname{diam}(D)]
\ge\sqrt2 B(1-2\gamma).
\]
Taking the infimum over all admissible \(D\) proves the first minimax inequality.

For the upper bound, define the fixed target parallelogram
\[
\mathcal P_B
=\{(x_1,x_2,x_1-x_2): |x_1|\le B,\ |x_2|\le B\}.
\]
If \(M'\in\mathcal M_{p,B}^{\mathrm{df}}\), then the coefficient restriction and the definition \(\alpha_e(M')=B_{e,XY}\) imply
\[
\tau(M')\in\mathcal P_B.
\]
The set \(\mathcal P_B\) is closed.  Hence the fiber closure in the definition of \(\Psi_B\), the union over the covariance region, and the final outer closure together imply, for every sample realization,
\[
\widehat{\mathcal C}^{B}_{n,\gamma}\subseteq\mathcal P_B.
\]
For two points of \(\mathcal P_B\), write \(u=x_1-y_1\) and \(v=x_2-y_2\).  Then \(|u|,|v|\le2B\), and
\[
\|(x_1,x_2,x_1-x_2)-(y_1,y_2,y_1-y_2)\|_2^2
=u^2+v^2+(u-v)^2
\le24B^2.
\]
Equality is attained by \((u,v)=(2B,-2B)\), so \(\operatorname{diam}(\mathcal P_B)=2\sqrt6B\).  Under the frozen convention an empty confidence set has diameter zero; therefore, pointwise,
\[
\operatorname{diam}(\widehat{\mathcal C}^{B}_{n,\gamma})
\le2\sqrt6B.
\]
Taking expectations and then the supremum over the bounded class proves the last inequality.  The coverage result already proved that \(\widehat{\mathcal C}^{B}_{n,\gamma}\) is admissible for the minimax infimum, so evaluating that infimum at this rule proves the middle inequality.

Finally, write \(R^*_{n,\gamma,B}\) for the displayed minimax value.  The established lower and upper bounds give
\[
\sup_{M\in\mathcal M_{p,B}^{\mathrm{df}}}
\mathbb E_M[\operatorname{diam}(\widehat{\mathcal C}^{B}_{n,\gamma})]
\le2\sqrt6B
=\frac{2\sqrt3}{1-2\gamma}\,
  \sqrt2B(1-2\gamma)
\le\frac{2\sqrt3}{1-2\gamma}\,R^*_{n,\gamma,B}.
\]
This is the claimed finite-sample constant-factor statement.  Nothing in the argument identifies the exact minimizer or exact minimax value, and neither bound depends on a separation or beta-min condition.
statements.justification: A coefficient-and-covariance-bounded Gaussian subclass converts the unrestricted noncontraction phenomenon into explicit finite-sample lower and upper expected-diameter constants while preserving exact-pivot coverage without separation assumptions.
statements.gap: The result supplies a certified constant-factor benchmark for the projected compatible-completion fiber; it does not claim an exact minimizer, an exact minimax value, or a sample-size contraction rate.
statements.consumer: The bounded theorem supplies a finite-width confidence union and quantifies its worst-case expected-diameter performance when scientifically defensible coefficient and covariance envelopes are available.

sampling_model.design: Two independent observational samples from centered positive linear-Gaussian acyclic SCM pairs in \(\mathcal M_p^{\mathrm{df}}\), with baseline-parent modular interventions and invariant innovation variances; the finite-diameter theorem separately restricts to \(\mathcal M_{p,B}^{\mathrm{df}}\).
sampling_model.units: Within environment \(e\), \(Z_{e1},\ldots,Z_{en_e}\) are independent and identically distributed; the two environment samples are independent.
sampling_model.treatment: \(X\) is an endogenous observed exposure; there is no randomized assignment.
sampling_model.overlap: Positive innovation variances imply positive-definite covariance matrices. The bounded subclass additionally imposes \(\kappa_B I_p\preceq\Sigma_{M,e}\preceq K_BI_p\), but neither class imposes a propensity-score, separation, strong-faithfulness, or beta-min condition.
sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: The observed nuisance is the covariance pair, while its exact equality/sepset ledger and compatible SCM completion fiber change discontinuously with that pair. The procedure inverts the exact paired Wishart pivot and recomputes the complete fiber throughout the covariance region; rational branch smoothness used in the limit proof is derived from positive-definite principal minors.

estimand_functional: The observed-law partial-identification map is \(s\mapsto\Psi(s)\), and inference projects the exact paired covariance region through that map: \(\widehat{\mathcal C}_{n,\gamma}=\overline{\bigcup_{s:\operatorname{vech}^{-1}(s)\in\mathcal R_{n,\gamma}}\Psi(s)}\). On the bounded subclass, the corresponding map is \(s\mapsto\Psi_B(s)\) and the projection is \(\widehat{\mathcal C}^{B}_{n,\gamma}\).
target_estimand: The primary causal target is the compatible-completion direct-effect fiber \(\Psi(s)=\overline{\{\tau(\widetilde M):\widetilde M\in\mathfrak F(s)\}}\). The fixed true causal triple is a retained member: \(\tau(M)\in\Psi(s(M))\) for every \(M\in\mathcal M_p^{\mathrm{df}}\).

tldr: This SCM partial-identification paper takes the compatible-completion direct-effect fiber \(\Psi(s)\), rather than a selected LDiffPC graph or point-identified coefficient, as its primary causal target. It proves a finite semialgebraic branch representation and projects an exact paired Wishart covariance region through every compatible diff-faithful completion, covering the fixed true direct-effect triple without equality, conditional-independence, beta-min, or completion-separation margins. Rational predecessor regressions imply branch smoothness on the positive-definite covariance domain, and tangent-cone regularity then yields zeroth- and first-order Fell random-set limits at simultaneous ledger boundaries. Same-law chain--fork witnesses prove every-dimension noncontraction and unrestricted infinite worst-case expected diameter, while an exact three-variable collider audit shows that unresolved structure can nevertheless yield a singleton fiber. On the separately declared coefficient/covariance-bounded Gaussian subclass, the same projection has exact finite-sample coverage and expected diameter within factor \(2\sqrt3/(1-2\gamma)\) of minimax. A compact-hyperspace kernel argument also attains each bounded Gaussian tangent decision problem as an exact semi-infinite variational benchmark, without producing an explicit optimizer or finite-sample dominance claim.

interpretation: The object \(\Psi(s)\) is the set of direct-effect triples compatible with one population covariance pair, the complete LDiffPC ledger, and the maintained SCM class. It can be a singleton or contain separated branch values; the paper does not identify the true triple by definition. The retention result proves \(\tau(M)\in\Psi(s(M))\), and the paired-Wishart event then lifts covariance coverage to coverage of that fixed causal member. At a ledger boundary the confidence union converges to the random collection of branch targets whose tangent cones meet the Gaussian acceptance body; when all accessible targets agree, the centered first-order set is the union of their derivative images. The bounded theorem shows that a nonshrinking but uniformly finite width can be information-theoretically appropriate even without a signal margin.
technical_internal_limitation: Exact covariance projection can be computationally expensive because every candidate covariance induces a fresh equality ledger and compatible-completion fiber; no fixed-treewidth algorithm, rejection certificate, or polynomial-time guarantee is proved. Tangent-cone regularity remains an asymptotic condition, although branch smoothness is derived from the rational predecessor-regression formulas and positive principal minors. The bounded Gaussian tangent infimum is attained and has an exact kernel semi-infinite-program characterization, but the work supplies neither an explicit minimizing rule nor a solved value, and it does not transfer that local result into finite-sample dominance. The bounded projected-Wishart union is only constant-factor minimax; exact minimax optimality or attainment of the finite-sample infimum is not claimed.
honest_scope: The primary target is the SCM compatible-completion fiber \(\Psi(s)\), with the fixed true triple retained as one member; point identification is not assumed. Exact finite-sample coverage ranges over positive diff-faithful baseline-parent modular interventions with invariant Gaussian innovation variances and requires no known ledger, unique order, unique branch, beta-min condition, or margin from non-diff-faithful boundaries. The bounded constant-factor result is stated only on the separately declared coefficient/covariance-bounded Gaussian subclass and gives no rate in sample size. The Fell limit is pointwise along \(N^{-1/2}\)-local sequences satisfying tangent-cone regularity; its branch smoothness and Taylor expansion are derived from the finite rational-branch theorem. The exact singleton collider audit is restricted to \(p=3\), whereas the chain--fork noncontraction witness holds for every \(p\ge3\). No componentwise uniform-single-door equivalence, fixed-treewidth algorithm, rejection certificate, latent-variable robustness, non-Gaussian exact positive inference, explicit local minimizer, finite-sample dominance, or exact minimax-optimality claim is made.
